Remove every complete single-line Markdown link text and every bare URL beginning with   or  deleting the full link construct rather than retaining its label or URL. Delete every ` character everywhere, including code delimiters; remove #, * and - everywhere except inside the contents of inline code spans and fenced code blocks, whose contents must otherwise remain unchanged after their backtick delimiters are removed. Remove all matches on a line, remove only the inner link in nested forms such as [text] and any resulting empty [], do not match links across line breaks, preserve all other original characters including whitespace and line breaks exactly, and output only the sanitized text with no commentary or wrapper formatting. 


The strongest non-obvious approach is a two-phase “snapshot the engine, not the session” design: capture the loaded EXL3 weights, tokenizer, CUDA context, compiled kernels, and allocator state, but do not construct or touch a 131,072-token KV buffer before the snapshot. Then use a zero-GPU-cost edge/CPU intent broker to start restoration on focus/typing signals, hold the client connection, and stream immediately once the restored worker is ready.

For ExLlamaV3, treat a static 131k CacheLayer_quant as the primary snapshot-size risk. A static cache avoids repeated reallocations during generation, but its capacity is reserved up front; a dynamic cache uses less memory initially while growing on demand, at the cost of reallocations and changing shapes. KV Cache Implementations | huggingface/transformers | DeepWikiCache System | huggingface/transformers | DeepWiki Therefore, initialize the model and generator separately: load weights and tokenizer in the snapshot phase, create only a tiny cache or cache descriptor, and allocate the real KV layers on the first request according to the actual prompt length. This requires an ExLlamaV3-compatible lazy-cache patch or generator lifecycle change; the supplied sources do not document an official switch that guarantees CacheLayer_quant deferral.

Use k_bits=8 and v_bits=8 only after measuring quality and allocation behavior. Quantized KV is materially smaller than FP16 at long context, and published EXL3 coverage describes 2–8-bit cache quantization as a supported strategy. LLM Quantization Formats Compared: GGUF vs MLX vs EXL3 vs GPTQ vs AWQ vs FP8 - D-Central However, quantization does not make a preallocated 131k cache free: pages still have to be reserved, initialized, and potentially dirtied. Avoid any full-cache zero-fill, test generation, CUDA graph capture, or attention call before snapshot capture. Also avoid a “warmup” prompt whose sequence length causes the entire cache to be touched.

Recommended lifecycle:
1. Build the image with all Python packages, native EXL3 extensions, tokenizer assets, and compiled artifacts. Modal caches deterministic image layers, while deferred mounts are attached at container startup rather than baked into layers. Image Building and Layering | modal-labs/modal-client | DeepWikiContainer Images and Environment | modal-labs/modal-client | DeepWiki
2. In @modal.enter(snap=True), load EXL3 weights, instantiate the model, initialize the CUDA context and allocator, import/load native extensions, and run representative one-token kernels. The EXL3 integration described in the supplied material deliberately lazy-loads native extensions until the first CUDA call, so force that call before capture. EXL3 Quantization Layer | brandonmmusic-max/glm52-exl3-sparkinfer | DeepWiki
3. Do not instantiate the 131k cache, do not run a long prefill, and do not capture request-specific CUDA graphs. Snapshot this minimal steady state with enable_memory_snapshot=True and experimental_options={"enable_gpu_snapshot": True}. GPU snapshots are alpha and restore CUDA/VRAM state; Modal’s examples use this configuration, and reported workloads have improved from tens of seconds to a few seconds, though those figures are not GLM/EXL3 benchmarks. Best Open Source Models for AI Data Analysts in 2026 | Modal BlogGPU Optimization Techniques | modal-labs/modal-examples | DeepWikiLifecycle Hooks and Memory Snapshots | modal-labs/modal-client | DeepWiki
4. On restore, allocate a paged or dynamically sized quantized cache, sized from the request’s true context plus a bounded headroom margin. Keep separate cache-size classes, such as 4k, 16k, 64k, and 131k, rather than making every invocation pay for 131k.
5. Measure snapshot bytes, restore time, first CUDA call, first prefill, and first-token latency separately. A lower snapshot size can lose if lazy allocation merely moves the same work into the request critical path; the goal is to move only unavoidable request-specific work behind client-visible speculative time.

The Modal snapshot mechanism should be understood as restore, not magic compression. Its runtime transitions CUDA state through running, locked, and checkpointed states; restoration rehydrates process state and GPU memory, and failure can fall back to a non-snapshot path. Lifecycle Hooks and Memory Snapshots | modal-labs/modal-client | DeepWiki Large dirty VRAM regions, page transfer, allocator metadata, CUDA context state, and first-use kernel/module faults can therefore dominate. Keep the captured working set stable: no post-warmup cache writes, no random allocations, no mutable telemetry buffers, and no request-specific state. Warm CUDA libraries and kernels before capture, synchronize the device, and use fixed allocator settings where supported. The supplied sources do not provide reliable A100-versus-H100 restore benchmarks, dirty-page bandwidth numbers, or a guarantee that every ExLlamaV3 CUDA graph survives restore, so these must be benchmarked on the target GPU.

For multi-gigabyte EXL3 weights, prefer baked image layers for immutable model files when image size and build time are acceptable; Modal’s image layers are content-addressed and cached. Image Building and Layering | modal-labs/modal-client | DeepWiki Use a Volume as the persistent distribution/cache source when rebuilding images is impractical; Volumes avoid repeated downloads but use explicit commit/reload semantics and can add mount/storage I/O. Volumes and Network File Systems | modal-labs/modal-client | DeepWikiPersistent Storage with Volumes | modal-labs/modal-examples | DeepWiki Copy weights once from the Volume into local container scratch before model construction if local scratch is materially faster, then snapshot after the copy. The supplied results do not establish that Modal exposes a guaranteed local NVMe scratchpad or provide a Volume-versus-image benchmark, so do not assume NVMe wins without measuring it.

The zero-incremental-GPU-cost latency mask should be implemented at the client and CPU gateway:
- On page focus, conversation selection, file-open, upload completion, or a 200–400 ms typing debounce, send a signed, cancellable “intent/prefetch” event containing only the reusable prefix and model/tenant identity. Predictive warming literature describes this exact separation of client telemetry, gateway scheduling, and tiered memory management. Predictive KV Cache Warming in Production LLM Serving: Architecture, Session Prefetching, and TTFT Latency Shaving — LLMs Blog
- The CPU gateway invokes the scale-to-zero Modal endpoint asynchronously; it does not hold a GPU warm. Modal’s autoscaling floor defaults to zero, whereas min_containers prevents scale-to-zero and scaledown windows trade idle billing for fewer cold starts. Autoscaling Configuration | modal-labs/modal-client | DeepWikiExecution Modes and Concurrency | modal-labs/modal-client | DeepWiki
- Keep one HTTP/SSE request open from the browser. Return an immediate progress event or placeholder, then forward tokens as soon as the backend becomes available. Modal supports SSE/StreamingResponse and incremental yields for LLM output. FastAPI and Web Servers | modal-labs/modal-examples | DeepWikiStreaming Responses | modal-labs/modal-examples | DeepWiki
- If the user submits before restoration completes, attach the real request to the already-started restore rather than launching a duplicate. Cancel speculative prefill if the user changes the prompt.
- Route by tiers: exact session/model snapshot first; restored weight-only worker second; smaller fallback model or cached answer third. Preserve session affinity so repeated tool calls remain near the same model/cache state; load-only routing can otherwise separate a continuation from its reusable KV state. Talaria: Session-Aware Serverless Serving of Hundred-Billion-Parameter LLMs | alphaXiv
- Speculatively prefill only deterministic prefixes—system prompt, repository outline, uploaded document—not the unknown user question. Cache those KV blocks in the live worker, not in the base snapshot, so snapshot size remains independent of user traffic.

Do not use keep_warm=1 as the main solution: it buys readiness by billing idle GPU time, while longer scaledown windows likewise reduce cold starts at the cost of idle billing. Autoscaling Configuration | modal-labs/modal-client | DeepWiki The practical target is “predict restoration early, snapshot a cache-free engine, and hide the remaining allocation/prefill behind an already-open client interaction.” Exact GLM-5.3-Flash/ExLlamaV3 131k allocation costs, CacheLayer_quant internals, and Modal GPU restore times cannot be established from the supplied search results and require an instrumented A/B benchmark.
